title: CXone APIs
blurb: Register, pick a grant, discover the tenant, and keep access keys smaller than the person who minted them.

lessons.title: Getting Started is a sequence
lessons.summary: The developer Getting Started path is plan, register, a test user, authentication, discovery, and best practices. Registration is typically a few business days. This lesson does not invent a portal SLA.
objectives: Use a test user before a production employee

p: Getting Started walks you through planning the integration, registering the application, creating a test user, choosing authentication, discovering your tenant's endpoints, and reading the best practices.
The portal's own pages are the contract. A blog that skips discovery and hard-codes a host is not.

Registration is reviewed. The Getting Started material describes that wait as typically a couple of business days. Treat any exact number of days as the current portal text, and re-read it before you promise a date.
The app lifecycle page is where you confirm what happens after registration. Do not invent an approval state the page does not list.

choices: Before you know which product you call
Should be re-read on the portal

lessons.title: Back-end apps use the password grant
lessons.summary: A back-end integration uses OAuth 2.0 resource-owner password credentials. client_secret_basic puts the client in the Authorization header. client_secret_post puts it in the body. The API user has no login authenticator.
objectives: Keep the API user off the login page

p: Back-end integrations on the authentication page use the OAuth 2.0 password grant. RFC 6749 defines that grant. The token request's username is the access key id and the password is the access key secret.

client_secret_basic sends the client id and secret in a Basic Authorization header. client_secret_post sends them in the body with grant_type=password. The registration form is where you chose which method the app uses.
The employee behind an API access key should not have a login authenticator. People sign in. Integrations present keys.
The key inherits that employee's permissions. The role should be the smallest one that can do the job. An administrator's key is an administrator.

steps.detail: A person's password is a different flow.

lessons.title: User-facing apps use OpenID Connect
lessons.summary: A user login uses the authorization code flow. scope is openid. response_type is code. Confidential clients then exchange the code. PKCE S256 is the proof for public clients. A password-grant sample pasted under that section is not the flow to teach.
objectives: Remember the only scope and response type

p: User-facing applications follow OpenID Connect. The authentication page says the only supported scope value for CXone API authentication is openid, and the only supported response_type for that login is code.
A confidential app then posts the code with client_secret_basic or client_secret_post. Public clients use PKCE. S256 is the method to use. OpenID Connect Core is the spec underneath.
The same authentication page also contains a token example that shows grant_type=password near the user-login discussion. That conflicts with the authorization-code branch above it.

This lab teaches authorization code for a person at a browser. The password grant stays in the back-end lesson. Treat the pasted password example in the user section as uncertain and do not copy it into a user app.

lessons.title: Discover the issuer, then the tenant
lessons.summary: Start at the global issuer or the FedRAMP issuer, append OpenID configuration, and read token_endpoint. The tenant id from the ID token selects the CXone configuration. Do not hard-code na1.

p: The global issuer on the authentication page is https://cxone.niceincontact.com. Append /.well-known/openid-configuration. A sample token_endpoint on that document is https://cxone.niceincontact.com/auth/token.
The FedRAMP Moderate issuer on the page is https://cxone-gov.niceincontact.com. Use the issuer your tenant belongs to.
After login, read tenantId from the ID token. Request {issuer}/.well-known/cxone-configuration?tenantId= that value.

A sample api_endpoint is https://api-na1.niceincontact.com with area na1 and domain niceincontact.com. The pattern is https://api-{area}.{domain}. Another tenant can be a different area. Hard-coding na1 is how a connector works in one region and fails in another.

choices: The same as commercial with no difference

lessons.title: Refresh early and pin the key id
lessons.summary: Plan to renew before 5 minutes of access-token expiry. expires_in of 3600 is a sample. Verify JWTs with JWKS, cache keys 15 to 30 days, and reject an unknown kid.

p: The token response includes expires_in. A sample on the page is 3600 seconds. The page also says each exchange can return a different lifetime, so you read the value you got.

The tip says to plan renewal of the refresh before 5 minutes of access-token expiry. A separate note allows up to 5 minutes of clock skew when you validate tokens. Those are two different five-minute rules.
Tokens are signed with NiCE's RSA keys. Fetch JWKS and cache the public keys for 15 to 30 days. Look in the cache first.

The kid in the JWT header must match a key in JWKS. An unknown kid is invalid. The page also says to cache unknown kids so you do not hammer the endpoint. Do not paste the documentation's sample JWT into a test; it carries sample claims.

steps.label: Clock skew
steps.detail: Up to 5 minutes is a different rule.

lessons.title: An access key secret is shown once
lessons.summary: If you miss the secret, mint another key. Disabling a key kills its tokens immediately. The key's power is the employee's power.

p: The access-key pages and the connector guides say the same thing: copy the secret when you create it. If you lose it, create a new key.
Disabling a key ends the tokens that key issued. There is not a grace period described on the manage-access-keys page.
Generate the key as the employee that should own the integration. Connector guides tell you to remove permissions from that role first.
A key created while you are signed in as a full administrator carries that administrator's permissions.

lessons.title: Studio API actions are not the whole catalog
lessons.summary: Some APIs have Studio actions. Verb colors are documented. If no action exists, the traditional path is Snippet or a REST call. GET NEXT EVENT is for agent-application events. Not every API has an action.
objectives: Fall back without inventing an action
Point agent events at GET NEXT EVENT

p: The API actions page colors verbs: POST green, PUT orange, GET blue, DEL red, PATCH aqua. A purple shield marks security.
Not every API has a Studio action. The page says to use Snippet or the REST API when an action does not exist. Online help for a specific action may be missing; the developer portal is the reference.
GET NEXT EVENT polls agent events for agent applications. It is not the token endpoint and it is not discovery.
This lab's script builder can place an API action for study. The JSON it exports is a classroom schema, not an import NiCE will load.
